While prior work has primarily focused on factual hallucinations, the structural characteristics of hallucinated reasoning remain insufficiently understood. This paper investigates diagnostic hallucinations through the lens of discourse structure and introduces a synthetic benchmark of ambiguous patient complaints paired with diagnoses, reasoning traces, discourse-tree representations, and hallucination labels. We hypothesize that hallucinated CoT differs from grounded reasoning not only in factual correctness but also in discourse organization. Our analysis shows that hallucinated reasoning tends to elevate weak or speculative clues into central discourse nuclei, suppress contradictory evidence, and use discourse satellites for post hoc reinterpretation rather than evidence integration. In contrast, grounded reasoning preserves alternative hypotheses, maintains explicit contrast and concession relations, and resolves evidential conflicts at higher discourse levels. Based on these observations, we formulate discourse-level indicators for hallucination detection and reasoning verification. {"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Acognitive+architecture+goal-directed+behavior+utility-reducing+blind+obedience+patterns+over-optimization&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: WEBCA: Weakly-Electric-Fish Bioinspired Cognitive Architecture
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1806.11401v1
published: 2018-06-29T13:22:37Z
summary: Neuroethology has been an active field of study for more than a century now. Out of some of the most interesting species that has been studied so far, weakly electric fish is a fascinating one. It performs communication, echo-location and inter-species detection efficiently with an interesting configuration of sensors, neu-rons and a simple brain. In this paper we propose a cognitive architecture inspired by the way these fishes handle and process information. We believe that it is eas-ier to understand and mimic the neural architectures of a simpler species than that of human. Hence, the proposed architecture is expected to both help research in cognitive robotics and also help understand more complicated brains like that of human beings.

title: An Initial Description of Capabilities and Constraints for a Computational Auditory System (an Artificial Ear) for Cognitive Architectures
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05332v1
published: 2022-02-10T21:23:17Z
summary: We present an initial set of factors, features, and constraints for developing a Computational Auditory System (CAS, aka less formally an artificial ear, AE) for use by cognitive architectures. We start to define a CAS and what tasks it should be able to perform. We then outline the features of a CAS for use by a cognitive architecture and factors that influence its performance. We conclude with an update on what has been created so far and insights on how to create and use a CAS in a cognitive architecture and include a set of functionalities for an artificial ear.

title: DAC-h3: A Proactive Robot Cognitive Architecture to Acquire and Express Knowledge About the World and the Self
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03661v2
published: 2017-06-12T14:39:43Z
summary: This paper introduces a cognitive architecture for a humanoid robot to engage in a proactive, mixed-initiative exploration and manipulation of its environment, where the initiative can originate from both the human and the robot. The framework, based on a biologically-grounded theory of the brain and mind, integrates a reactive interaction engine, a number of state-of-the-art perceptual and motor learning algorithms, as well as planning abilities and an autobiographical memory. The architecture as a whole drives the robot behavior to solve the symbol grounding problem, acquire language capabilities, execute goal-oriented behavior, and express a verbal narrative of its own experience in the world. We validate our approach in human-robot interaction experiments with the iCub humanoid robot, showing that the proposed cognitive architecture can be applied in real time within a realistic scenario and that it can be used with naive users.

title: Using a cognitive architecture to consider antiBlackness in design and development of AI systems
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00644v3
published: 2022-07-01T19:39:13Z
summary: How might we use cognitive modeling to consider the ways in which antiblackness, and racism more broadly, impact the design and development of AI systems? We provide a discussion and an example towards an answer to this question. We use the ACT-R/Φ cognitive architecture and an existing knowledge graph system, ConceptNet, to consider this question not only from a cognitive and sociocultural perspective, but also from a physiological perspective. In addition to using a cognitive modeling as a means to explore how antiblackness may manifest in the design and development of AI systems (particularly from a software engineering perspective), we also introduce connections between antiblackness, the Human, and computational cognitive modeling. We argue that the typical eschewing of sociocultural processes and knowledge structures in cognitive architectures and cognitive modeling implicitly furthers a colorblind approach to cognitive modeling and hides sociocultural context that is always present in human behavior and affects cognitive processes.", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "54ab0caba68d6deb2c4ab5cfff4583fc374fc6aae65755b6bfa768ba6896af7f", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "obedience_limits", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["arxiv:1806.11401v1", "arxiv:2202.05332v1", "arxiv:1706.03661v2", "arxiv:2207.00644v3"], "source_candidates": [], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing
general
-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice
questions
(MCQs) and
open
-
ended
question
answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance,
scientific
validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809
questions
with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems.
Open
resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing
general
-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice
questions
(MCQs) and
open
-
ended
question
answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance,
scientific
validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809
questions
with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems.
Open
resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

▽ More
AI scientists are expanding automated research across
scientific
domains, yet their ability to turn the
scientific
record into a foundation for
autonomous
discovery
remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five
agentic
systems powered by large language models and six third-party
agent
harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what
scientific
papers communicate and what
autonomous
agents
require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual
Agents
(RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new
scientific
papers to be continuously incorporated.

AI coding
agents
are increasingly used for
scientific
work, but their end-to-end
autonomous
research capability remains difficult to verify. We present ResearchClawBench, a benchmark for evaluating
autonomous
scientific
research across 40 tasks from 10
scientific
domains. Each task is grounded in a real published paper, provides related literature and raw data, and hides the target paper during evaluation. Expert-curated multimodal rubrics decompose the target
scientific
artifacts into weighted criteria, enabling evaluation of target-paper-level re-
discovery
while leaving room for new
discovery
. We evaluate seven
autonomous
research (auto-research)
agents
under a unified protocol and seventeen native LLMs through the lightweight ResearchHarness. Current systems remain far from reliable re-
discovery
: the strongest
autonomous
agent
, Claude Code, averages 21.5, and the strongest ResearchHarness LLM, Claude-Opus-4.7, averages 20.7, with an LLM frontier mean of only 26.5. Error analysis shows that failures concentrate in experimental protocol mismatch, evidence mismatch, and missing
scientific
core. ResearchClawBench provides a reproducible evaluation frontier for measuring progress toward
autonomous
scientific
research.
